questions.question: A client has vomiting, deep breathing, high blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, and metabolic acidosis, but glucose is only moderately elevated. What is the best interpretation?
choices: DKA remains possible, including euglycemic DKA
DKA is excluded unless glucose exceeds 600 mg/dL
The pattern proves isolated HHS
Ketones cannot cause acidosis when glucose is modest
questions.explanation: DKA is identified by clinically significant ketosis and acidosis with diabetes or hyperglycemia; SGLT2 inhibitors and illness can produce DKA without marked glucose elevation.

questions.question: Which presentation most strongly suggests HHS rather than predominantly DKA?
choices: Profound dehydration, very high glucose and osmolality, altered mentation, and little major ketoacidosis
High ketones with marked acidosis and only modest glucose
Isolated low glucose after insulin
Normal mentation and normal osmolality
questions.explanation: HHS is characterized by severe hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with profound water loss and often neurologic dysfunction, without the prominent ketosis and acidosis of DKA.

questions.question: A client with DKA has potassium 3.2 mmol/L before insulin begins. Which risk is most urgent?
choices: Insulin may lower potassium further and cause dangerous dysrhythmia or weakness
Potassium is always high throughout DKA treatment
The low potassium proves DKA has resolved
No potassium reassessment is needed after fluids
questions.explanation: A potassium below 3.5 mmol/L requires replacement and a delay in insulin under the adult consensus pathway until corrected, because insulin can rapidly worsen hypokalemia.

questions.question: Why can a client with DKA have a normal or high serum potassium at presentation despite a total-body deficit?
choices: Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis causes overall losses
A normal serum value means no potassium has been lost
Urine production stops all potassium loss
Ketones always increase total-body potassium stores
questions.explanation: The circulating value can be misleading: cellular shifts raise serum potassium even as urinary losses deplete total stores. Treatment reverses shifts and may reveal dangerous hypokalemia.

questions.question: An older adult with HHS also has heart failure and crackles. Which fluid-management approach is safest?
choices: Follow individualized fluid orders with frequent perfusion, breathing, and urine-output reassessment
Give the same large fixed fluid rate as every younger client
Avoid assessing the lungs because HHS always causes dehydration
Stop all perfusion monitoring once glucose falls
questions.explanation: HHS requires restoration of circulation, but heart failure raises overload risk. The RN follows the individualized prescription and repeatedly evaluates perfusion and respiratory tolerance.

questions.question: During DKA treatment, glucose falls substantially while ketones and acidosis remain. What should the RN anticipate under the prescribed protocol?
choices: Dextrose may be added while insulin continues until ketoacidosis resolves
Stop all insulin immediately because glucose improved
Discharge the client based on glucose alone
Ignore ongoing ketones because urine glucose is lower
questions.explanation: Insulin must continue to suppress ketogenesis until biochemical resolution. Dextrose may be added to prevent hypoglycemia while ketones and acidosis clear.

questions.question: Which new finding during HHS treatment requires urgent neurologic reassessment?
choices: A new seizure or declining level of consciousness
A gradually improving heart rate with stable mentation
Improved thirst after fluids
Urine output returning toward baseline
questions.explanation: HHS and its treatment involve large osmotic shifts. New seizure, headache, focal change, or falling consciousness requires immediate evaluation rather than routine observation.

questions.question: Which finding best supports DKA resolution?
choices: Glucose alone reaches a near-normal value
Clinical recovery with ketone and acid–base resolution under the protocol
Urine ketones remain positive without other information
One improved blood-pressure reading
questions.explanation: DKA resolution depends on recovery of ketonemia and acidosis with clinical improvement. Glucose can normalize before ketogenesis has fully stopped.

questions.question: A client with DKA reports that insulin ran out because it was unaffordable. Which prevention plan best addresses the cause?
choices: Document nonadherence and provide no further assessment
Arrange access to insulin and supplies, teach a written sick-day plan, and coordinate follow-up with the care team
Tell the client to use a neighbor's insulin indefinitely
Focus only on the inpatient glucose result
questions.explanation: Preventing recurrence requires resolving the access barrier, ensuring the regimen and supplies are available, and teaching individualized sick-day and emergency actions.

questions.question: When transitioning a recovered client with type 1 diabetes from IV to subcutaneous insulin, what is essential?
choices: Stop the infusion hours before any basal insulin is given
Coordinate prescribed basal coverage and overlap so there is no gap in insulin effect
Replace insulin with fluids alone
Use A1C as the only criterion for stopping IV insulin
questions.explanation: An appropriate overlap between IV insulin and subcutaneous basal insulin helps prevent rebound hyperglycemia and recurrent ketosis, especially in type 1 diabetes.
